claims.text: Kutch Ajrakh is an elaborate resist block-printing technique built on a series of direct and resist printing and dyeing steps.

quotes.quote: Kutch Ajrakh is an elaborate resist block printing technique that involves series of direct and resist printing and dyeing to create unique effects.
Ajrakh is a unique combination of hand block printing and resist dyeing.

claims.text: Ajrakh is a double-sided block-printed textile worn as caste dress by cattle herders in Kachchh, Thar and Sindh, where Khatri artisans make it.

quotes.quote: Ajrakh is a double-sided, block-printed textile worn as caste dress by cattle herders in the desert regions of Kachchh and Thar in north-west India and Sindh in Pakistan, where it is made by Khatri artisans.

claims.text: The Kutch Ajrakh tradition is kept up in three villages of Kutch district, Ajrakhpur, Dhamadka and Khavda.

quotes.locator: Application 1050, geographical area and proof of origin, p. 8
quotes.quote: The Ajrakh traditions are maintained in three villages of Kutch district namely Ajrakhpur, Dhamadka and Khavda.
The production of Ajrakh is now restricted to only three centers, namely Dhamadka, Khavda and Ajrakhpur.

claims.text: Traditional ajrakh uses four colours, blue, black, red and white, and a piece needs all four to be called ajrakh.

quotes.quote: Traditionally four colours were used i.e., blue, black, red and white.
For a piece to be called ajrakh, it needs to have all the four colours, blue, red, black and white.
is traditionally blue with red, black, and white patterns of classic Islamic style

claims.text: Ajrakh has become the signature cloth of the Khatri communities of Dhamadka and Ajrakhpur in Kachchh and their most successful product.

quotes.quote: it has also become the signature cloth of the Khatri communities at Dhamadka and Ajrakhpur in Kachchh and is their most successful product.

claims.text: The process and designs of ajrakh printing are shared by Sindh, now in Pakistan, by Kutch and by Barmer district of Rajasthan.

quotes.locator: Application 1050, geographical area and proof of origin, p. 8
quotes.quote: The process and designs of Ajrakh printing are common to Sindh (now in Pakistan), Kutch and Barmer district of Rajasthan.

claims.text: The origin of ajrakh can be traced to Sind, now in Pakistan, from where the printing came to Kutch.

quotes.quote: The origin of ajrakh can be traced to Sind, Pakistan.
The origin of Ajrakh can be traced to Sind, Pakistan.

quotes.locator: Application 1050, geographical area and proof of origin, p. 8
quotes.quote: Ajrakh printing originally came from Sindh and got concentrated where extra soft water was available.

claims.text: Ajrakh artisans belong to the Khatri community, Hindu and Muslim, and most artisans of Kutch and Barmer believe their ancestors came from Sindh.

quotes.quote: The artisans who made these textiles belonged to the Khatri community (both Hindus /Muslims)
Most of the artisans of Kutch and Barmer believe that their ancestors were from Sindh, and even now many of their relatives live in the Sindh region.
Originally from Sindh, the Khatris practice crafts like block print, batik print, tie and dye, and rogan painting.

claims.text: Rao Bharmalji I of Kutch, who ruled from 1586 to 1631, invited Khatri cloth printers from Sindh and gave them land and freedom from tax.

quotes.quote: The erstwhile ruler of Kutch Rao Bharmalji - I (1586-1631), invited the cloth-printing Khatri artisans from Sindh and gave them permission to settle and earn their livelihoods anywhere in Kutch.
They were given land by the state as well spared any taxation on their produce.

Rao Barmalji I, the King of Kachchh, was a patron of craft. He invited artisans from across Sindh to come and settle in his kingdom. We were given land and accommodations. Even the taxes were cancelled for us.
The respondent mentioned that Raja Bharmalji I of Bhuj had brought the artisans from Sindh, Pakistan to this part of Gujarat.
Rao Bharmalji, a ruler of sixteenth-century Kutch and patron of the arts, brought the Khatris to his kingdom.

claims.text: Many Khatri printers of Dhamadka and Ajrakhpur descend from Jindha Jiva, who founded Dhamadka during the reign of Rao Bharmal I, and share the Dhadha clan.

quotes.quote: many of the Khatri ajrakh printers in Dhamadka and Ajrakhpur are closely related, descended from a common forefather, Jindha Jiva, who founded Dhamadka during the reign of Rao Bharmal I of Kachchh (r. 1586-1631) - they belong to the same (Dhadha) clan.

claims.text: Popular legend dates the tradition to 1586, when Raja Bharmal I invited the forefathers of Mohammad Siddiki to move from Sind to Dhamadka.

quotes.quote: According to popular legend, this textile tradition was started in the family of late Mohammad Siddiki when in the year 1586, Raja Bharmal I, invited his forefathers, to migrate from Sind and settle in Dhamadka, Kachchh.

claims.text: The GI application states that ajrakh work went on at Dhamadka for the past 450 years because a stream of the Indus gave it water.

quotes.locator: Application 1050, geographical area and proof of origin, p. 8
quotes.quote: The Ajrakh activities prevailed at Dhamadka since the past 450 years, as it was having a potential water source from one of the water stream of the Indus river.

claims.text: Block printers identify the trefoil on the shawl of the Mohenjo-daro priest-king bust with kakar, the cloud motif of ajrakh.

quotes.quote: A trefoil pattern is carved into his shawl. Block printers will identify the trefoil motif as kakkar, a cloud pattern common to the traditional Ajrakh patterns made in Sindh and Kachchh.
The celebrated statue of the King Priest discovered at Moenjodaro has a trefoil motif on the draped shawl. The ajrak craftsmen claim that the pattern is kakar, a cloud pattern.
The bust of the Priest King of Mohenjo Daro depicts him wrapped in a shawl with trefoil motifs, similar to the kakar or cloud motif seen in ajrakh prints.

claims.text: In 1930 hundreds of Indian cotton fragments of the 11th to 14th century were found at Al Fustat in Old Cairo, the earliest known printed cloth.

quotes.quote: In 1930, hundreds of Indian cotton fragments from the 11th-14th century AD were discovered in Al Fustat, the harbor of Old Cairo.
They remain the earliest example of block printed cloth.
In 1930, hundreds of cotton fragments were retrieved from Al Fustat - harbor of Old Cairo - dating from the 11th to the 14th century AD. These fragments are the earliest known printed textiles.

claims.text: The Fustat fragments, simple patterns printed with small blocks and resist dyed in indigo and madder, bear a striking similarity to ajrak.

quotes.quote: The simple patterns printed with small sized blocks, resist dyed in indigo and madder, bear a striking similarity to ajrak.
The Al Fustat textiles were printed using small blocks, natural colors, and simple patterns. Similar designs are still being printed in modern-day Dhamadka and Ajrakhpur.

claims.text: Khatri Mohammed Siddik, who had practised chemical dyeing since it entered ajrakh in 1950, began experimenting with natural dyes in 1975 from memory of his father's practice.

quotes.locator: section 3.5, Mohammed Siddik Khatri and family, p. 76
quotes.quote: After having practiced chemical dyeing since it was introduced into ajrakh in 1950 (Abdulrazak Khatri, e-mail communication August 2011), Khatri Mohammed Siddik began experimenting with natural dyes in 1975 with what he had remembered of his father's practice

claims.text: Mohammad Siddik of Dhamadka, whose extended family dominates ajrakh printing, won the National Award in 1981.

quotes.locator: section 3.5, Mohammed Siddik Khatri and family, p. 79
quotes.quote: The National Award, following Mohammed Siddik in 1981, has been won by Abdulrazak in 1998, Abdulrahim Abdulrazak in 2002, Abduljabbar in 2003, and Haroon Rashid Abdulrazak in 2006.
The domination of the craft by a single extended family, that of the late Mohammad Siddik of Dhamadka, is noteworthy
In 1981, our father Khatri Mohammad Siddik received a national award for a natural dyed bedsheet.

claims.text: Ajrakh was first adapted for soft furnishings in the mid-1970s and quickly became popular in urban India.

quotes.quote: First adapted for use as soft furnishings in the mid1970s, ajrakh quickly became popular in urban India.

claims.text: In 2001 an earthquake that caused severe damage in Kutch almost destroyed Dhamadka, which lay only 20 km from the epicentre.

quotes.quote: In 2001, an earthquake which caused severe damage in Kutch almost destroyed the village of Dhamadka.
Dhamadka village was only 20 km from the epicentre and was decimated by the earthquake

claims.text: After the 2001 earthquake the block printers of Dhamadka moved 40 km away, in search of good quality groundwater, to a new village named Ajrakhpur.

quotes.locator: Application 1050, geographical area of production, p. 8
quotes.quote: After a massive earthquake in Kutch in 2001, the block printers were forced to relocate. They settled in Ajrakhpur village.
moved from their earlier settlement in Dhamadka to their present location, 40 km away, in search of good quality groundwater
They aimed to look for a place with good quality groundwater. Thus they came to their present address, and the village was named Ajrakhpur

So people from our village came together and bought land 40 kms away from Dhamadka. One member was identified from ten main families who would together take key decisions. We called the new village Ajrakhpur.

claims.text: Ajrakhpur was established in May 2001 as the Khatri community's model of best craft practice after the Gujarat earthquake.

quotes.quote: The village established in May 2001 represents the endeavours of the Khatri community of Kachchh to create a model of best craft practice and to rise from the devastation wrought by the Gujarat earthquake.

claims.text: Ajrakhpur, developed after the 2001 earthquake for the printers of Dhamadka with Gujarat government support, lies 12 km from Bhuj.

quotes.quote: Post the earthquake in 2001, with the efforts of Ismail Khatri and other printers and with the support of the Government of Gujarat, a village called Ajrakhpur, 12 km from Bhuj, was developed exclusively for the printer community of Dhamadka.

claims.text: In Kachchh the cloth is soaked at least three times in neerani, an emulsion of castor oil, soda ash and camel dung, and left to steep overnight.

quotes.quote: these dried plums contain high levels of Tannic acid.
The tannin in the Myroballan penetrates the cotton fibres and is essential pre-mordant which aids the adhesion of the subsequent printed mordants onto the cloth.

claims.text: Stage 3, rekh or khariyanu, prints the white outlines of the design with a carved block and a resist paste of lime and gum, usually in the morning.

quotes.quote: 3 Rekh (outline) printing: Gum arabic and lime are mixed for kiryana (printing of the white outlines).
Preparation of Outline of design (Khariyanu/ Kiriyana):- Outlines of the design, where white is required, are printed with a carved wooden block and a resist paste containing lime and tree gum.
The morning time is usually preferred for this stage of printing.

claims.text: For double-sided ajrakh the outline is printed again on the reverse with rekh blocks, matched precisely with the help of small registration marks on block corners.

quotes.quote: If the fabric had to be printed double sided, then they are printed on the reverse side with rekh blocks.

When double sided Ajrakh is printed it is essential that the same outline design be printed on the reverse of the cloth. A printer must be very accurate to ensure designs match precisely on both the sides and the fabric should be partly wet to ensure proper registration.
This is helped by small registration marks on the corners of the symmetrically patterned blocks.

claims.text: Lime in the outline resist discharges alum, so the pa paste must not touch khariyanu areas or no red will develop in the later dyeing.

quotes.quote: Care must be taken not to mix this Pa with the areas printed in lime Khariyanu otherwise the lime will discharge the alum and thus prevent colour developing during subsequent red dyeing.
this must not spread onto areas where red is required or the lime will discharge the subsequent applications of alum.

claims.text: Contemporary ajrakh uses a resist of lime, which is calcium hydroxide, and gum from the babul tree, Acacia nilotica indica.

quotes.quote: a paste made of lime (calcium hydroxide) and gum from the babul or acacia tree (Acacia nilotica indica)
The latter resist is used for contemporary ajrakh
Gum and lime are the most preferred resit materials today by the Ajrakh block printers.
While Ajrakh and most related cloths are resist printed with a gum arabic and lime substance

claims.text: Stage 4 dries the outline-printed cloth in the sun, turning it over to dry the other side when both faces will be printed.

quotes.quote: 4 Drying of rekh printed fabric: After printing the fabric with rekh (outlines), the fabric is dried in sun and if the fa bric is to be printed both the sides, the fabric is reversed to dry on the other side.

claims.text: Stage 5, kat, prints black with a paste once made of gum, ferrous sulphate and fuller's earth, now of scrap iron, tamarind seed powder and jaggery.

quotes.quote: 5 Kat (black) printing: Gum, ferrous sulphate, fuller's earth and water are used to make the black outlines.
These ingredients were traditionally used but today, the process of kat printing is carried out using scrap iron, kachuka no loat (tamarind seeds powder) and gud (jaggery) to make paste.

claims.text: The GI journal describes kut as a fine paste of jaggery or molasses in which scrap iron and gram flour have fermented for ten to fifteen days.

quotes.quote: The kut is a smooth finer paste made from jaggery, or molasses, in which scrap iron such as horse-hoes and besan (gram flour) have been fermented for ten to fifteen days.
Scrap iron, jaggery and tamarind is soaked in water for two weeks and then cooked over flame to create the black dye for Ajrakh.

claims.text: The iron, jaggery and gram flour mixture for kat ferments in about one week in the hot season and two weeks in the cold season.

quotes.quote: This mixture is left to ferment which takes about one week in the hot season and two weeks during the cold season; a yellowish scum on the surface of the mixture indicates that it is ready for use.

claims.text: On harde-treated cloth kut turns a deep, fast chocolate-black as the iron in the paste oxidises with the tannic acid.

quotes.quote: When printed onto the harde treated cloth kut develops a deep fast chocolate-black colour as the iron particles in the kut paste oxidise with the tannic acid.
These lines oxidise when exposed to air and the harda and develop a black colour.

claims.text: Stage 6, phulli or kan, stamps small star-like areas with tamarind seed powder boiled in alum, tinted with a fugitive dye, kesari rang; traditionally geru was used instead.

quotes.quote: 6 Phulli/Kan printing: Resisting of small star like areas, where Kachuka no lot (tamarind seeds powder), is mixed in alum and then boiled for 1 hr to produce a thick printing paste.
To this, some amount of fugitive dye, k esari rang, is added to separate this paste from the other printed resist pastes.
Traditionally, geru is used instead of fugitive dye. The fabric is now stamped with this paste.

claims.text: Pa, the red mordant paste, is alum suspended in boiled tamarind seed powder and printed on mavi, the parts of the design that must be red.

quotes.quote: The mordant, alum required for producing red is now applied to the cloth. Alum is suspended in a sticky paste of boiled powder from roasted and ground tamarind seeds (locally known as kachika).

This smooth paste called Pa, is printed with blocks which have been carved so that the printing portion of the raised face is patterned only, with the areas of the design called mavi, where red is required.

claims.text: Stage 7, gach, stamps a khor resist of alum, gum arabic, millet flour and red clay, then a resist of lime and gum arabic, dusted against smudging.

quotes.quote: 7 Gach/ Khor printing: The first part of this stage is called khor printing, where the resist is prepared with a paste of alum, gum arabic, millet flour and red clay and is stamped on the fabric with the help of filler block ( gadh).
The later step of this stage includes the stamping of resist paste made of lime and gum arabic.
traditionally powder of dried Bakri ni lindi (goat excreta) is sprinkled, which prevent the smudging of design.

claims.text: In gach paste the clay and millet flour resist indigo, while its alum acts as a mordant for the red dye applied later.

quotes.quote: The clay and millet flour in the paste act as a resist, preventing indigo from staining the cloth beneath, whilst the alum content acts a mordant for subsequent application of red dye.

claims.text: Stage 8 dyes the cloth in indigo for 10 to 15 minutes, traditionally in a naand dug into the ground where indigo and casatoria seeds ferment for months.

quotes.quote: 8 Indigo dyeing I: Traditionally, natural indigo is used and the naand ('V' shaped container), that was dug in ground is used for dyeing.
The indigo along with kuwadia na beej (casatoria seeds) is added in naand containing water and is left for months for the growth of bacteria. Then, the fabric is dyed in it for 10-15 min.

claims.text: Synthetic indigo is set in a clay maat with sodium hydrosulphite and caustic soda and is left to mature for 3 to 4 days.

quotes.quote: Today, the synthetic indigo is put along with sodium hydrosuphite and caustic soda in the maat (clay container) containing water. The maat is left to mature for 3-4 days

claims.text: Clifford records a natural indigo vat of indigo, sagikhar salt, lime, casiatora seed and water, fermented for about one month, sometimes with jaggery.

quotes.quote: In order to establish an indigo vat, natural indigo, sagikhar (a salt), lime, casiatora (seed from kuwada plant) and water are mixed in a clay vessel, plastic barrel or concrete vat.
The dye bath is left to ferment for about one month; sometimes jaggery is added to this to aid fermentation.

claims.text: Cloth lifted from the indigo vat is bright green at first and turns blue as oxygen meets the dye on the fibres.

quotes.quote: At first bright green, the cloth rapidly becomes blue as oxygen meets the dye particles on the fibres.
The dyed cloth emerges a bright green that slowly turns blue once the dye oxidises.

claims.text: For the darkest blues the cloth may be dipped three or four times in the indigo vat, and it is reprinted between dips when two blue shades are wanted.

quotes.quote: If a design required the darkest shades of the blue then the cloth may be subjected to a total of three or four immersions into the vat to build up rich blue.
if two shades of the blue are required in the design then cloth is reprinted between the immersions into the Indigo vat, to preserve areas of the lighter blue achieved from the first dip.

claims.text: Stage 9, vichharnu, washes the indigo-dyed cloth in running water without hard rubbing, so the khor resist stays and the cloth remains stiff.

quotes.quote: 9 Vichharnu: The indigo dyed fabric is washed in running water and laid flat to dry in sun. Fabric is not vigorously rubbed and the khor resist is not removed and hence the resultant fabric remains stiff.

claims.text: Stage 10, rang, boils the cloth for 2 to 3 hours with tamarisk galls and madder in the charu pot of the rangchul, then washes and sun-dries it.

quotes.quote: 10 Rang: For this step, the cloth is boiled with dhaori na phool (galls of tamarisk) and majith (madder) with sufficient amount of water in the charu of rangchul (metal container fixed on a stand) for 2-3 hrs.
The fabric is then washed in running water and dried in sun.

claims.text: For red, alizarin crystals or madder roots are heated gently in a large copper pot over a low fire, and dyeing the purest reds takes up to four hours.

quotes.quote: Alizarin crystals or the crushed and steeped roots of majeeta or Indian Madder are gently heated in a large copper pot.
The fire beneath is kept low and the lengths of cloth continuously
Dyeing the purest reds continues for up to four hours.

claims.text: Karolia and Buch record that steps 7 to 10 are repeated once more to give brighter and more brilliant shades of red and blue.

quotes.quote: Steps 7 to 10 are repeated once again to get brighter and more brilliant shades of red and blue.

claims.text: In Clifford's record stage 11 repeats the gach alum printing and is called minakari, a Persian word for enamelling used in Kachchh for double work.

quotes.quote: 11. Gach (alum printing - see 7) is repeated. The cloth is left for several days after this. This stage is known as minakari (from Persian, refers to enamelling but used in Kachchh to mean 'double work')

claims.text: The long thin roots of Indian madder, Rubia cordifolia or majeeta, give a dye that binds to the alum mordant and develops red where pa and gach were printed.

quotes.quote: Indian Madder roots, Rubia Cordifolia, locally known as majeeta, have been traditionally used in the creation of Ajrakh
This dye extracted from these long thin roots links to the alum mordant on the cotton fibres and develops red area of a design, where Pa, Gach pastes have been printed.

claims.text: Alizarin, among the first chemical red dyes, was invented in 1868 by German chemists Graebe and Liebermann and quickly superseded madder.

quotes.quote: Alizarin was one of the first chemical dyes for red, invented in 1868 by German chemists Graaebe and Liebermann.
Derived from coal tar this crystalline red dye rapidly superseded madder, its natural counterpart.

claims.text: Despite being synthetic, alizarin still needs a mordant such as alum to attach its colour to the cotton fibres.

quotes.quote: Despite its chemical synthesis, alizarin dye also requires mordants such as alum to attach its colour to the cloth fibres.

claims.text: Edwards writes that synthetic alizarin and German indigo are chemically identical to the natural dyestuffs but far cheaper, reliable and easy to use.

quotes.quote: uses synthetic forms of madder (alizarin) and indigo ('German indigo')
chemically identical to the natural dyestuffs but far cheaper, they are easy to use, reliable and available in large quantities.

claims.text: Natural madder roots hold more complex colour compounds than synthetic alizarin, so madder dyeing often leaves a pinkish tinge on the white areas.

quotes.quote: The color compounds contained within natural madder roots are much more complex than those of synthetic alizarin. As a result dyeing with majeeta often leaves a pinkish tinge to the white areas of a design.

claims.text: In tapano, madder-dyed cloth was soaked in camel dung, spread on sandy river banks and kept moist for at least three days so sun and dung bleached the whites.

quotes.quote: The dyed cloth would be soaked in a solution of camel dung, then spread on the sandy banks of a river in the sun and regularly sprinkled with water to keep it moist throughout the day.
This would be repeated over at least three days, by the end of which the sun, moisture and various compound in the dung would have acted as a bleaching agent on the white areas of a design.

claims.text: Karolia and Buch describe ajrakh printing as a laborious process of 14 stages, each needing different tools and ingredients.

quotes.quote: The process of ajrakh printing is laborious and includes 14 stages. Each stage requires different tools and ingredients.
Appendix A: Fourteen Stages of Ajrakh

claims.text: The GI journal counts 15 to 16 stages of dyeing and printing in ajrakh, taking approximately 15 to 21 days.

quotes.quote: In total, 15-16 different stages are involved in the process of dyeing and printing, which take approximately 15-21 days.

claims.text: Ajrakh is also described as a water-intensive 16-stage process, with one step done each day before the cloth is rested.

quotes.quote: It is a water-intensive, 16-stage process that takes time and is much in demand among Indian and international buyers.
The cloth is made in a sixteen step process of washing, dyeing, printing, and drying, with one step being performed in one day and the fabric being put to rest for the day.

claims.text: Ajrakh blocks are wooden because wood absorbs colour evenly; blocks for the first stage of printing are shisham, those for the third and fourth stages teak, and idle blocks are soaked in mustard oil.

quotes.quote: The artisans use only wooden blocks in preparing Ajrakh print as wood absorbs the color better and more uniformly. The blocks used in the first stage of printing are made of shisham and the blocks used in the third and fourth stages are made of teak.
The blocks are soaked in mustard oil when not in use so that they do not expand in the rainy season.

claims.text: Blocks are carved in pairs so each registers an exact inverted image on the reverse; in Sindh these pors are cut from local Acacia arabica.

quotes.quote: The pors are carved from the Acacia Arabica trees, indigenous to the Sindh region.
The blocks are carved in pairs that can register an exact inverted image on the other side.
The printing blocks are often carved in pairs, thus registering an exact inverted image on the other side of the cloth.

claims.text: The rangchul dyeing tank was built of bricks and cow dung, and its charu pot was traditionally made of aluminium.

quotes.quote: The equipments, like rangchul (tank for dyeing) were made using bricks and cow dung. Charu (pot in the rangchul) was made traditionally out of aluminium.

claims.text: The GI journal lists ajrakh's raw materials as harda, scrap iron, tamarisk galls, casatoria seeds, sajikhar salt, madder, alizarin, alum, turmeric, dried pomegranate, jaggery, tamarind seed powder and indigo.

quotes.quote: The ingredients are water, Terminalia chebula Retz. (harda; myrobalan), lokhand (scrap iron), dhaori na phool (galls of tamarisk), kuwadia na beej (casatoria seeds), sajikhar (salt), majith (madder), alizarine, fatakdi (alum),

Curcuma domestica Valeton (haldar; turmeric powder), Punica granatum Linn. (dadam; dried pomegranate), gud (jaggery), Tamarindus indica Linn. (kachuka no lot; powdered tamarind seeds), natural indigo/synthetic indigo, sodium hydrosulphite and caustic soda (if synthetic indigo used)

claims.text: Ajrakh is printed mainly on cotton bought in counts from 60's to 120's depending on its end use, and silk ajrakh is made to order.

quotes.quote: The artisans procure cotton fabric ranging from 60's to 120's count depending upon the end use of the product from the market.
Silk Ajrakh is also prepared by artisans for customized needs
Ajrakh Print is predominantly prepared by using cotton fabrics and natural dye.

claims.text: Most ajrakh dye materials are found locally and prepared by the dyers, with some supplied by cattle herders and others bought from Ayurveda practitioners.

quotes.quote: Most of the dye materials used are locally available in the region. Usually, these are sourced and prepared by the dyer. Some are supplied by local cattle herder and others are procured from Ayurveda practitioner.

quotes.locator: section 'We work in harmony with nature'
quotes.quote: Various flowers, myrobalan fruit, pomegranate skin, natural soda ash were all obtained locally for preparing the dye.

claims.text: Green ajrakh is made by dipping indigo-dyed cloth in pomegranate and then spraying or swabbing it with turmeric solution while damp.

quotes.quote: leelo (green colour) is obtained by dipping the indigo dyed fabric in pomegranate and then spraying or swabbing haldi (turmeric) solution on the fabric. This was done when the fabric was still damp.
Green: Indigo/ Neel and Pomegranate/ Dadam or Turmeric/ Haldi

claims.text: Harde is a yellow astringent paste from the dried powdered fruits of the myrobalan tree, Terminalia chebula, widely used in ayurvedic medicine.

quotes.quote: The soft cleaned cloth now undergoes a soak in Harde, a yellow astringent paste made from the dried powdered fruits of the Myroballan tree, Terminalia Chebula. Used widely in ayurvedic medicines

claims.text: Ajrakh indigo is either natural indigo from the plant Indigofera tinctoria or a synthesised substitute known as German indigo.

quotes.quote: Indigo dye can either be natural Indigo from Indigofera tinctoria, or a synthesized substitute "German" indigo.

claims.text: Indigofera tinctoria, once cultivated on a vast commercial scale in India, is now confined to a few areas, chiefly around Tindivanam in Tamil Nadu.

quotes.quote: Once widely cultivated on a vast commercial scale in India, indigo (L. Indigofera tinctoria) is now confined to a few areas, the chief centre at present being Tindivanam, Tamil Nadu.

claims.text: The GI application reads ajrakh's palette as the universe, with red for the earth, black for darkness, white for clouds and blue for the universe.

quotes.quote: Ajrakh art took inspiration from the universe due to its colour palette. Red goes for Earth, Black for Darkness, White for Clouds and Blue for the Universe itself.

claims.text: Karolia and Buch record blue as the sky, red as the light of sunset, white as the stars and black as the dark night.

quotes.quote: Vadali / neela stands for blue colour signifying sky; laal: stands for red, which signifies the red light in the sky at the time of sunset. Safed / dhodo is white colour used for stars; kalo, the black colour signifies dark night;

claims.text: Ajrakh design follows mizan, the Islamic principle of balance and order, and its design square is divided into quarters and then sixteen parts.

quotes.quote: The foundation of Islamic art is Mizan, which meas balance and order. This principle also governs the design and pattern of Ajrakh . The design square is perfectly divided into quarters and then further divided into sixteen parts
patterns of classic Islamic style, based on mizan (balance or order) and geometry.

claims.text: Traditional ajrakh has a fixed layout, a large central field of a motif repeated on a tight grid, framed by borders and end panels.

quotes.quote: Traditional Ajrakh textiles have a fixed layout. They feature a large central body, with a repeated motif on a tight grid, border and end panels.
Both ends of the cloth are decorated while three sides have embellished borders, whose designs are fixed. Only the motif in the centre of the cloth may be changed.

claims.text: Abduljabbar M. Khatri of Dhamadka, a leading producer, counts between twenty-five and thirty traditional ajrakh designs in regular use.

quotes.quote: today include between twenty-five and thirty designs, according to Abduljabbar M. Khatri of Dhamadka, one of the leading producers of ajrakh in Kachchh.
Although Abduljabbar M. Khatri at Dhamadka estimates the range of ajrakh patterns in regular use to be between twenty-five and thirty designs

claims.text: The GI application says ajrakh once had more than fifty designs, but by the mid 90s only 15 designs were counted as ajrakh.

quotes.quote: In older times there were more than fifty designs but by mid 90s there were only 15 designs which categorized as Ajrakh,

claims.text: An ajrakh is a rectangle of two stitched parts with fixed borders on all sides and a field carrying one of about sixteen patterns.

quotes.quote: An Ajrakh, a rectangular cloth, made in two parts stitched together, has a fixed set of multiple borders on its long and short sides, and a field with one of about sixteen patterns.
We have a portfolio of 16 traditional ajrakh designs

claims.text: Each ajrakh pattern is built from three blocks, an outline called rekh and two filling blocks called datlo, one for each colour.

quotes.quote: Each pattern is created with impressions of three blocks, an outline called rekh, and two filling patterns called datlo-one for each color; all patterns must register.

claims.text: Traditional char pa ek blocks built a motif from four registered impressions, but faster sal type blocks carrying the whole motif have replaced them.

quotes.quote: Traditional blocks, called char pa ek (four parts to one), in which motifs are created by registering four impressions, have been abandoned for a style called sal type (flush joining), in which the entire motif is on one block.
Printing with these blocks is faster, though less perfect-suited for cheap, scaled-up production.

claims.text: A 2006 ajrakh turban cloth by Ismail Mohammad Khatri in the V&A carries the cloud design called kakar.

quotes.quote: Ajrakh turban cloth with cloud design, designed and made by Ismail Mohammad Khatri, Gujarat, 2006
The cloud design is called kakar.

claims.text: A 2006 ajrakh shawl in the V&A has repeating red, white and black star-like patterns on indigo, made of two 90 cm panels sewn together.

quotes.quote: Ajrakh shawl, repeating red, white and black star-like pattern on indigo ground, designed and made by Ismail Mohammad Khatri, Gujarat, 2006
Made up of two panels each 90 cm wide sewn together vertically.

claims.text: Ajrakh designs are geometrical patterns based on squares, with stars, circles and ellipses set symmetrically within them, in deep blue and red.

quotes.quote: The designs are restricted to a range of geometrical patterns based on squares, with stars, circles and ellipses arranged symmetrically within them.
The traditional colouring of Ajrakh is deep blue and red, with a small amount of white and black.
Ajrakh can still be recognized for its intricate star shaped patterns interspersed into geometric borders and its deep indigo hues.

claims.text: Traditional ajrakh is stitched along its centre because cloth was once woven in narrow widths, and such cloth is called bi-poti ajrakh.

quotes.quote: This magnificent textile has a peculiar characteristic of being stitched from centre. The reason for this was, earlier the fabrics were woven in to small width and hence to produce a normal width of fabric, small pieces of fabric were stitched together.
The fabric so produced of ajrakh was called Bi-poti ajrakh.
Earlier, when the fabric used was woven on the pit looms, the required width of fabric was acquired by joining two narrow width lengths with use of a decorative joining stitch.

claims.text: Ajrakh printed on one side is ek-puri and on both sides bi-puri, and identically printed bi-puri cloths were the most highly prized.

quotes.quote: Ajrakh is of two types - ek-puri, which is printed only on one side and bi-puri, which is printed on both sides.
The most highly prized Ajrakh textiles were bipuri, i.e. the ones printed identically on both sides.

claims.text: The most acclaimed ajrakh, minakari, is double-faced, and its alignment is tested by holding the finished cloth up to the sun to reveal mistakes.

quotes.quote: the most acclaimed is a double-faced textile, printed on both sides of the fabric, dyed using madder and indigo, and known as minakari.
tested by holding the finished cloth up to the sun, thus revealing any mistakes, requires the utmost skill on the part of the artisan.

claims.text: Legends say ajrakh was printed on both sides because Maldhari men dressed before sunrise to herd livestock and were unable to tell right side from wrong in the dark.

quotes.locator: section 'Ajrakh is what we are known for'
quotes.quote: Legends say this was made because the Maldhari men needed to get dressed before the sun rose in order to herd their livestock.
would leave their homes even before sun rise and there was no electricity in those times so they couldn"t differentiate the right side from the wrong side in darkness.

claims.text: Printing and dyeing both sides twice gives deeper indigo and madder, extends the cloth's life and leaves no reverse side showing on a turban or shoulder cloth.

quotes.quote: In the most traditional version, the fabric is painstakingly printed on both sides with exact registration, dyed, washed, and then printed on both sides and dyed again.
This creates deeper shades of indigo and madder, extends the life of the cloth, and enables it to be used as a turban or shoulder cloth in which no reverse side shows.

quotes.quote: in the Geographical Indications Journal 188 dated December 19, 2023
is hereby advertised as accepted under Sub-section (1) of Section 13

claims.text: The GI Registry issued the certificate of registration for Kutch Ajrakh, application 1050, a Gujarat handicraft, on 22 April 2024.

quotes.quote: 1050 - Certificate of Registration - 22-04-2024 | 22/04/2024
643 1050 Kutch Ajrakh Handicraft Gujarat

claims.text: The Kutch Ajrakh GI application was facilitated by the Textiles Committee of the Ministry of Textiles, Government of India.

quotes.quote: Facilitated By: Textiles Committee, Ministry of Textiles, Government of India

claims.text: Khatri printers knew their clients through hereditary relationships and bartered their dyed cloth directly with them for milk, animals and grain.

quotes.quote: Khatris knew their clients intimately, usually through hereditary relationships, passed down through generations.
They bartered their dyed fabrics directly to their users for milk, animals, and grain.
They used the barter system and exchanged cloth for produce from farmers, while cattle herders gave them milk or ghee.

claims.text: Muslim Maldhari cattle herders, the traditional purchasers of ajrakh in Kutch, wore it as a lower wrap, a turban and a shoulder cloth.

quotes.quote: Muslim Maldhari men, or cattle herders, wore Ajrakh as a poth (lungi, or lower wrap), turban, and shoulder cloth
The traditional purchasers of Ajrakh were Muslim nomadic animal-keepers, a group that still survives. In Kutch (Gujarat) this community is referred to as Maldharis.

quotes.locator: section 'Ajrakh is what we are known for'
quotes.quote: Ajrakh is the traditional attire of the Muslim Maldharis, the pastoral communities from the region. An Ajrakh turban was a gift for the Maldhari groom at the time of marriage.

claims.text: Khatri printers of Kutch have almost stopped printing ajrakh for Maldharis, who buy cheaper screen-printed cloth in chemical dyes, mostly from Pakistan and from Khavda.

quotes.quote: These days the Khatri artisans of Kutch have almost stopped producing Ajrakh prints for their traditional Maldhari customers
because of the entry of screen-printed material using chemical dyes, mostly from Pakistan and locally from the village of Khavda in Kutch, which due to their low prices have become very popular
has meant that Khatri craftsmen have almost stopped producing Ajrakh for the Maladharis.

quotes.locator: section 'We have walked all over the Banni'
quotes.quote: Maldharis still wear Ajrakh cloth today. However, due to change in practices, the traditional hand block printed, natural dyed Ajrakh is no longer affordable for them. They purchase either the screen-printed substitutes or the Ajrakh block prints from Sindh.

claims.text: In 2014 Abduljabbar M. Khatri's workshop made 70,000 m of cotton running yardage for Fabindia, which with Maiwa Handprints is his largest client.

quotes.quote: His annual production for Maiwa in 2014 included 1,000 m of 'running cotton'
Production for Fabindia in the same year included 70,000 m of 'running yardage' in cotton
Maiwa Handprints based in Vancouver, Canada, and Fabindia based in New Delhi, India. They are his largest clients

claims.text: Edwards writes that ajrakh's popularity brings threats from the screen-printing industry centred on Jaipur, which reproduces traditional block prints for a fraction of the cost.

quotes.quote: the current popularity of ajrakh also brings threats from the screen-printing industry centred on Jaipur, which reproduces traditional block prints for a fraction of the cost

claims.text: Synthetic blue and red dyes now usually replace natural indigo and madder, but the traditional processes and number of stages are kept.

quotes.quote: Although synthetic blue and red dyes are now usually used in place of natural indigo and madder, the processes followed are still the traditional ones.

The production process has not changed in the number of stages but there is a change in the natural ingredients used at different stages. Natural indigo had been replaced by synthetic indigo to cut down on the time of production.

claims.text: Scholars believe the word ajrakh derives from the Arabic azrak, meaning blue, and this is its most commonly accepted origin.

quotes.locator: section 'Ajrakh is what we are known for'
quotes.quote: Scholars believe that Ajrakh is derived from the Arabic word azrak, which means blue.
more popularly the term seems to be derived from Azrak, which means blue in Arabic.
the Arabic origin of the word - from azraq, meaning "blue" or "indigo" - is the most commonly accepted.

claims.text: Local Kachchhis and artisans say the name ajrakh means aaj rakh, keep it for today.

quotes.locator: section 'Ajrakh is what we are known for'
quotes.quote: According to local Kachchhis, Ajrakh means "keep it today."
Artisans say that its name means aj rakh (leave it for today).
The popular story among local practitioners is that Ajrakh means "keep it today"

claims.text: Karolia and Buch note the term ajrakh may have evolved from the Sanskrit jharat, from which a-jharat, a stable object, was coined.

quotes.quote: The term Ajrakh may have been evolved from the Sanskrit word, Jharat from which A-jharat (stable object) was coined

claims.text: The etymology of the word ajrakh is contested, with several legends of origin and a question of Arabic, Sindhi or Sanskrit roots.

lede.text: Kutch Ajrakh is an elaborate resist block-printing technique of direct and resist printing and dyeing, made by Khatri artisans as a double-sided textile.
Its tradition is kept up in the Kutch villages of Ajrakhpur, Dhamadka and Khavda, and its process and designs are common to Sindh, where it originated, and to Barmer district of Rajasthan.
A traditional piece needs all four colours, blue, black, red and white, and the most highly prized cloths were printed identically on both sides.

sentences.text: The origin of ajrakh is traced to Sind, and Rao Bharmalji I of Kutch invited Khatri printers from Sindh and gave them land and freedom from tax.
Many Khatri printers descend from Jindha Jiva, who founded Dhamadka in the reign of Rao Bharmal I, and Dhamadka and Khavda became the main centres of ajrakh in Kachchh.
Indian cotton fragments of the 11th to 14th century found at Al Fustat in Old Cairo were printed with small blocks in simple patterns that bear a striking similarity to ajrak.
Mohammed Siddik, who had practised chemical dyeing since 1950, began experimenting with natural dyes in 1975 and won the National Award in 1981.
Ajrakh was first adapted for soft furnishings in the mid-1970s and quickly became popular in urban India.
In 2001 an earthquake almost destroyed Dhamadka, and its block printers moved 40 km away, in search of good quality groundwater, to a new village named Ajrakhpur.
The cloth is first scoured in saaj by repeated soaking in castor oil, soda ash and camel dung and drying until it is soft and white, though sources differ on whether these ingredients are still used.
In kasanu it is treated with harda (myrobalan), and the white outlines are then printed with rekh blocks in a resist of gum arabic and lime.
Kat prints the black with an iron paste, and kan or pa prints a paste of alum and tamarind seed powder where red is required.
Gach printing adds a resist of alum, gum arabic, millet flour and red clay before the cloth is dyed in indigo and washed in running water.
In rang the cloth is boiled with tamarisk galls and madder, or dyed with alizarin crystals, and steps 7 to 10 are repeated for brighter red and blue.
Sources count 14, 15 to 16 or 16 stages, and the GI journal gives approximately 15 to 21 days for the whole process.
Sources differ on when the first red dyeing comes: the GI journal puts the madder or al dyeing straight after the alum pa printing, before the gach resists and indigo dyeing.
Myrobalan contains high levels of tannic acid, an essential pre-mordant that aids the adhesion of the printed mordants onto the cotton.
Printed on harde-treated cloth, kut develops a deep fast chocolate-black as the iron in the paste oxidises with the tannic acid.
Madder and synthetic alizarin both need alum as a mordant to develop red, and lime in the outline resist discharges the alum.
Cloth lifted from the indigo vat is bright green and turns blue as oxygen meets the dye on the fibres.
Water rich in alum, tin or chrome brightens the colours, while iron in the water supply dulls and darkens the final result.
Sources differ on whether synthetic alizarin is chemically identical to natural madder, whose colour compounds the GI journal finds much more complex.
Most dye materials are locally available and prepared by the dyer, with some supplied by cattle herders and others bought from Ayurveda practitioners.
The GI journal lists harda, scrap iron, tamarisk galls, casatoria seeds, sajikhar, madder, alizarin and alum, with turmeric, pomegranate, jaggery, tamarind seed powder and indigo.
Contemporary ajrakh uses a resist of lime and gum from the babul tree, while gach uses alum, gum arabic, millet flour and red clay.
The cotton is procured in counts from 60's to 120's depending on the end use, and silk ajrakh is prepared for customized needs.
Traditionally the red dyeing is done with madder or al root, whichever is available.
Edwards writes that the River Suran served Dhamadka until the late 1980s, and the GI journal records that its water stream dried up in 1989.
After the 2001 earthquake Dhamadka's water held more iron, which saddens dye colours, and even one percent of iron leaves black spots on myrobalan-dyed cloth.
Ajrakhpur was chosen for good quality groundwater, but its water table is going down and excess iron and rising salinity threaten the craft again.
Khamir set up a pilot effluent treatment plant in 2007, and in 2022 the government launched an effluent treatment system at Ajrakhpur.
Ajrakh printing is also practised in Barmer, though Kachchh cloths are finer, and Sindh has its own centres of ajrak.
Khatri printers knew their clients through hereditary relationships and bartered their dyed cloth directly with them for milk, animals and grain.
Khatri printers of Kutch have almost stopped printing ajrakh for Maldharis, who buy cheaper screen-printed cloth in chemical dyes, mostly from Pakistan and from Khavda.
In 2014 Abduljabbar M. Khatri's workshop made 70,000 m of running cotton yardage for Fabindia, one of his largest clients with Maiwa.
Ajarakhpur Hastkala Vikas Sangathan applied to register Kutch Ajrakh as a geographical indication under application 1050, and the certificate of registration followed in 2024.
In 2011 only fifteen of the forty-five Khatris still in Khavda worked on ajrakh, all of them with chemical dyes.
Ajrakh design follows mizan, the Islamic principle of balance and order, with the design square divided into quarters and then sixteen parts.
A fixed layout sets a large central body of a repeated motif on a tight grid within borders and end panels.
Block printers identify the trefoil on the Mohenjo-daro priest-king's shawl with kakar, the cloud motif of ajrakh.
The most acclaimed ajrakh, minakari, is printed identically on both sides, and its alignment is tested by holding the cloth up to the sun.
